headline: A Google medical chatbot that interviewed patients before urgent primary-care visits needed no safety stops in 98 supervised chats, in what researchers believe is the first real-world study of its kind.
score_reason: Peer-reviewed, first real-world test of a patient-facing medical chatbot; small, single-hospital and feasibility only, so no change from the curator score.
importance_line: A patient-facing chatbot ran safely under live physician watch, which matters to patients and primary-care doctors, but 98 supervised chats at one hospital, funded by Google's parent Alphabet, do not show better health outcomes.
summary: Researchers at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, working with Google, report in The Lancet that their AMIE chatbot interviewed patients by text before urgent primary-care appointments, and none of the 98 completed conversations needed a physician to step in for safety. A supervising doctor logged one hallucination, and the study tested feasibility only, not whether the tool improves patients' health.
notes: The New York Times original was blocked (403); written from the BIDMC release carried by Newswise, which describes the same Lancet trial (inferred match on topic and date). Study funded by Alphabet.
